title: Why I Started Coding
hook: I didn't fall in love with coding, I grew into it.
body:
I didn't start out chasing a passion for programming. I started because I wanted to build things and Python
was the easiest way in. The first few weeks were slow: syntax errors, confusing tutorials, and a lot of
copy-pasting without fully understanding why something worked. What changed things was consistency, not
talent. Showing up daily, even for 30 minutes, taught me more than any single course. Over time, Python led
me into web development, automation, AI, and eventually mobile and IoT projects. None of that felt possible
on day one.
lesson: Consistency beats motivation. Small daily effort compounds faster than short bursts of enthusiasm.
benefit: This mindset is the foundation behind every project I will share in the next 30 days.

title: The First Python Script That Actually Worked
hook: My first useful Python script was ten lines long, and it felt like magic.
body:
It was nothing impressive: a script that renamed a folder full of files based on a pattern. But it solved a real
annoyance, and that made the difference. Before that, I was writing code just to finish exercises. This was
the first time code did something for me. It used a loop, a function, and basic file handling. That is it. But it
taught me that programming is really about solving small, boring problems before it becomes about anything
advanced.
lesson: You don't need advanced skills to write useful code. You need a real problem to solve.
benefit: The same loop-and-function logic later became the core of bigger automation scripts I built.

title: Git Saved My Project (and My Sanity)
hook: I lost two days of work before I actually understood why version control matters.
body:
Early on, I kept multiple folders like project_final, project_final2, project_actually_final. Then one bad edit
broke something and I had no way back. That is when I properly learned Git: commits, branches, and writing
messages that actually describe what changed. It felt like extra work at first. Now I cannot imagine starting a
project without it, whether I am working alone or with a team.
lesson: Version control is not optional, even for solo projects. It is a safety net you will eventually need.
benefit: Every project since then, from Flutter apps to FastAPI backends, has been tracked in Git from day one.

title: Building My First Real Web Page
hook: Before any framework, I built plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript pages, and I am glad I did.
body:
It is tempting to jump straight into React or Next.js, but starting with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
helped me understand what frameworks are actually doing underneath. I learned the box model, how the
DOM updates, and why layout bugs happen in the first place. Later, when I started using Tailwind CSS,
styling became much faster, but the fundamentals I learned first are still what I rely on when something
breaks.
lesson:
Learn the fundamentals before the framework. Frameworks are shortcuts, not replacements for
understanding.
benefit: This foundation made it much easier to debug UI issues later in bigger web applications.

title: Why I Moved to React and Next.js
hook: Plain JavaScript got messy fast once my projects grew past a few pages.
body:
Managing state and repeating UI code across pages became a real headache. Moving to React, and later
Next.js, gave me reusable components, cleaner structure, and routing that just made sense. It was not about
following a trend. It was about my projects outgrowing what plain JavaScript could handle cleanly. Next.js in
particular helped once I needed things like server-side rendering and simpler routing.
lesson: Pick your tools based on what the project actually needs, not what is popular.
benefit: React and Next.js now power the dashboards and admin panels in my SaaS-style projects.

title: My Backend Journey: From Node.js to FastAPI
hook: I started backend development with Node.js, then fell for FastAPI.
body:
Node.js was a natural next step after JavaScript on the frontend, and it worked well for general APIs. But
once I started building AI-related backends, FastAPI made more sense. It is Python-based, so it fits naturally
with AI and data libraries, and its automatic request validation and docs save real time. I did not abandon
Node.js, I just started choosing the right tool for each project.
lesson: There is no single best backend. The right choice depends on what the project connects to.
benefit: FastAPI now powers most of the AI APIs and backend services I build.

title: Choosing Between MongoDB and Firebase
hook: I used to think all databases were basically the same. They are not.
body:
MongoDB gives me more control and flexibility for custom backend systems, especially when the data
structure is more complex, like inventory or school records. Firebase, on the other hand, is great when I
need quick real-time sync, especially for Flutter mobile apps, without setting up a full backend. Learning
when to use which one saved me a lot of unnecessary backend work.
lesson: Choose your database based on the project's needs, not habit.
benefit: MongoDB backs my management systems, Firebase backs several of my Flutter apps.

title: My First Automation With n8n
hook: I automated a repetitive task in one afternoon and felt silly for not doing it sooner.
body:
I had a simple but annoying task: manually copying form submissions into a spreadsheet and sending a
notification. With n8n, I built a workflow that did it automatically, connecting a trigger to a couple of actions
with no custom backend needed. It was one of those moments where I realized how much time gets wasted
on tasks that do not need a human at all.
lesson: Look for repetitive, rule-based tasks first. Those are the easiest and most valuable to automate.
benefit: This same workflow-building approach now supports parts of the AI assistant projects I build.

title: Why I Started Learning Flutter
hook: I wanted one codebase for Android and iOS, so I picked Flutter.
body:
Maintaining separate native apps was never realistic for me as a solo developer. Flutter, using Dart, let me
write one codebase and ship to both platforms. The learning curve was real, especially understanding
widgets and how everything is a widget in Flutter. State management was confusing at first too. But once it
clicked, building mobile UIs became genuinely enjoyable.
lesson: Cross-platform tools can save enormous time for solo developers and small teams.
benefit: Flutter became my main tool for building real mobile apps, not just prototypes.

title: Building My First Real Flutter App
hook: My first Flutter app crashed more than it worked, and I learned more from that than any
body:
I built a simple utility app early on, and it kept crashing due to poor state management and layout mistakes I
did not fully understand yet. Debugging it, widget by widget, taught me more about Flutter than any course
did. I learned how state actually flows through widgets, and why keeping UI logic separate from business
logic saves so many headaches later.
lesson: Debugging a broken project teaches you more than following a perfect tutorial.
benefit: Those early mistakes shaped how I now structure every Flutter app I build.

title: UI/UX Is Not Just Making Things Pretty
hook: I used to think good design meant nice colors. I was wrong.
body:
Good UI/UX is really about how easily a user can do what they came to do. I learned this the hard way after
building a screen that looked nice but confused every test user. Now, before touching colors or fonts, I think
about user flow: what does someone need to see first, and what should be one tap away. Visual design
comes after that, not before.
lesson: Usability comes before visual polish. A confusing interface fails no matter how good it looks.
benefit: This shift in thinking directly improved the usability of my pharmacy and school management systems.

title: Building a Pharmacy and Medical Store Management System
hook: A local pharmacy still tracking stock on paper inspired one of my most useful projects.
body:
I built a management system to handle inventory, sales, and expiry date tracking for a small pharmacy or
medical store setup. The goal was simple: reduce manual errors and make it easy to see what is low in
stock or close to expiry before it becomes a problem. It combines a web interface with a backend and
database to keep records organized and searchable instead of scattered across notebooks.
lesson: The best project ideas usually come from watching a real, everyday problem, not from a tutorial list.
benefit: It directly reduces manual stock errors and expiry-related losses for small medical stores.

title: Designing a School Management SaaS
hook: Schools still manage attendance and fees on paper more often than people realize.
body:
This project is built as a SaaS-style system with different roles: admin, teacher, and student, each seeing
only what they need. It handles attendance, fee tracking, and basic record keeping in one place instead of
spreadsheets and paper registers. Designing for multiple user roles was the hardest part, since each role
needed a different view of the same data without exposing information they should not see.
lesson: Building for multiple user roles means designing permissions and views from day one, not adding them later.
benefit: It reduces manual admin work and keeps attendance and fee records in one accessible system.

title: Building AI APIs With FastAPI
hook: Connecting an AI model to a real API taught me things no course covered.
body:
Calling a model in a notebook is easy. Serving it reliably through an API is a different problem entirely. I
used FastAPI to wrap AI functionality into clean endpoints, handling request validation, response formatting,
and basic error handling along the way. Response time and stability mattered just as much as the AI output
itself, something I had not fully appreciated before building this.
lesson: Production AI work is mostly backend engineering. The model is only one part of the system.
benefit: This backend pattern now powers the AI assistant and automation projects I build.

title: What Basic Cybersecurity Taught Me About My Own Code
hook: Learning basic cybersecurity made me go back and rewrite parts of my own projects.
body:
Once I started learning the basics of cybersecurity, like input validation, authentication practices, and
common vulnerabilities, I realized some of my earlier projects had gaps I had not even considered. Things
like trusting user input without checking it, or storing data without thinking about who could access it. It
changed how I approach every new project, not just security-focused ones.
lesson: Security is a mindset you build into every project, not a feature you add at the end.
benefit: My APIs and web apps are noticeably more careful about input handling and access control now.

title: A Small Cybersecurity Project That Taught Me a Lot
hook: I built a simple tool to test basic security weaknesses, and it changed how I write code.
body:
As part of learning cybersecurity basics, I built a small tool to check for common weaknesses, like weak
password patterns and simple input handling flaws in a test application. It was a basic, educational project,
not a professional security audit. But actually seeing how easily a poorly validated form can be exploited was
far more effective than reading about it.
lesson: Hands-on security practice teaches lessons that theory alone cannot.
benefit: It made me more careful with authentication and input handling in every project since.

title: My First Steps Into Computer Vision
hook: The first time OpenCV detected a face on my webcam, I stared at the screen for a full minute.
body:
Computer vision felt like a completely different world coming from web and app development. Starting with
OpenCV, I learned how images are just arrays of numbers, and how operations like grayscale conversion,
edge detection, and basic face detection actually work under the hood. It was less about magic and more
about understanding pixels, matrices, and the math behind them, with NumPy doing a lot of the heavy lifting.
lesson: Computer vision starts with understanding data, specifically pixels and arrays, not with fancy models.
benefit: This foundation made every computer vision project after this one much easier to understand.

title: Building a Real-Time Object Tracking Project
hook: I built a project that could track movement in real time using nothing but a webcam.
body:
Using OpenCV and NumPy together, I built a project that detects and tracks moving objects through a live
camera feed. It involved frame differencing, contour detection, and a fair amount of tuning to reduce false
detections from lighting changes. NumPy handled the array operations behind the scenes, which made the
processing fast enough to run in real time.
lesson:
Combining a vision library with proper array processing is what makes real-time computer vision actually
usable.
benefit: This kind of tracking logic applies directly to monitoring and simple automation use cases.

title: Hand Tracking With MediaPipe: My First AR Experiment
hook: I moved a virtual object on screen using just my hand, no mouse, no keyboard.
body:
MediaPipe made hand tracking far more approachable than I expected. It gave me hand landmark points in
real time, which I used to detect gestures and control an on-screen element. Getting the landmarks was the
easy part. Turning raw coordinates into smooth, reliable gesture detection took more tuning than I
anticipated.
lesson: Gesture-based and touchless interfaces are more accessible to build today than most people assume.
benefit: This experiment became the base for a more complete AR and hand-tracking project.

title: Building an AR and Hand-Tracking Project
hook: I built an interface you control with hand gestures instead of touching anything.
body:
Combining OpenCV and MediaPipe, I built a project where hand gestures control on-screen actions, like
selecting, dragging, or triggering an action without touching a mouse or screen. The real challenge was not
detecting the hand, it was making the interaction feel smooth and predictable rather than jumpy and
frustrating.
lesson: Combining computer vision models with a clear practical use case is what turns a demo into a real project.
benefit: This kind of touchless control has real applications in interactive kiosks and accessibility tools.

title: Why I Got Into IoT and ESP32
hook: I wanted my code to control something in the real world, not just a screen.
body:
After spending most of my time in software, I wanted to see code affect something physical. The ESP32 was
a natural entry point: cheap, capable of Wi-Fi, and well supported. I started with basic sensor readings and
simple outputs, learning how to think about timing, power, and hardware limitations, which is very different
from software-only development.
lesson: IoT forces you to think about hardware constraints, not just logic and code.
benefit: This opened the door to building real physical automation and monitoring projects.

title: Building an ESP32-Based IoT System
hook: I connected a microcontroller to the internet and controlled a device from my phone.
body:
Using an ESP32, I built a project that reads sensor data and sends it over Wi-Fi, along with the ability to
control an output remotely. Getting stable Wi-Fi connectivity and handling reconnections turned out to be
trickier than the actual sensor logic. It taught me that reliability matters more than features in IoT projects.
lesson: In IoT, a system that reconnects reliably is more valuable than one packed with extra features.
benefit: This same pattern applies to home automation and small-scale industrial monitoring setups.

title: Designing a Web HCI for Industrial Motors
hook: An industrial motor doesn't care about your UI, until someone has to operate it every day.
body:
I worked on a web-based human-computer interface for monitoring and controlling industrial motor
parameters. Unlike a typical consumer app, the priority here was clarity and reliability over visual flair.
Operators needed to see critical values at a glance, with minimal chance of misreading a control or a status
indicator, since a mistake here is not just inconvenient.
lesson: Industrial software design prioritizes simplicity, clarity, and reliability far above aesthetics.
benefit: It makes day-to-day motor monitoring and control safer and easier for operators.

title: What I Learned Connecting Hardware to a Web Dashboard
hook: Getting a motor's real sensor data to show up correctly on a web page took longer than
body:
Bridging ESP32-based hardware with a web dashboard involves more than just sending data. I had to
handle inconsistent readings, connection drops, and making sure the frontend did not break when data was
delayed or missing. This kind of hardware-to-web integration debugging is a very different skill from typical
frontend or backend work.
lesson: Hardware-software integration requires patience with unpredictable, real-world data, not just clean code.
benefit: This pattern is reusable across different IoT dashboard projects, not just the motor system.

title: Getting Started With Agentic AI
hook: I built an AI setup that didn't just answer questions, it took actions.
body:
Agentic AI is different from a normal chatbot in that the model can use tools, call functions, or trigger actions
based on a goal instead of just returning text. I started experimenting with this by giving a model access to a
small set of defined tools it could call when needed. It changed how I think about AI, less like a search
engine, more like a component in a larger system.
lesson: Agentic AI is about giving models the ability to act within limits, not just generate text.
benefit: This concept now sits at the core of the AI assistant projects I am building.

title: Running Local LLMs With Ollama
hook: I ran an AI model on my own machine, no API key, no internet required.
body:
Ollama made it straightforward to download and run open models locally. For certain projects, this matters a
lot, especially when privacy, offline access, or cost is a concern. It is not a replacement for larger hosted
models in every case, but for many practical tasks, a local model running through Ollama is more than
enough.
lesson: Local LLMs give you more control, privacy, and predictability for the right kind of project.
benefit: This makes offline or privacy-sensitive AI assistant features realistic to build.

title: Building an AI Assistant With Automation
hook: I connected an AI model to my daily workflow using n8n.
body:
A useful AI assistant is rarely just a chat window. I connected an AI model to an n8n workflow so it could
trigger actions based on a request, instead of only replying with text. This combination of AI reasoning and
automation logic is what actually makes an assistant useful for repetitive digital tasks, rather than just a
novelty chatbot.
lesson: A real AI assistant needs automation and tool access, not just a capable language model.
benefit: This setup saves real time on repetitive digital tasks I used to do manually.

title: The Biggest Mistakes I Made as a Developer
hook: I once shipped a project without testing it properly, and it broke in front of someone who
body:
Looking back, most of my early mistakes were avoidable: skipping proper testing, ignoring version control
discipline, and over-engineering simple features because I wanted to use a new tool. None of these
mistakes were dramatic on their own, but together they cost real time and, occasionally, real trust. The
lesson was not to avoid mistakes entirely, but to actually reflect on them instead of repeating the same ones.
lesson: Mistakes are the fastest teacher, but only if you take the time to reflect on why they happened.
benefit: Recognizing these patterns early has meant fewer repeated mistakes in every project since.

title: How All These Skills Actually Connect
hook: People sometimes ask why I learn so many different things instead of picking one.
body:
Web development, mobile apps, AI, computer vision, IoT, and cybersecurity might look unrelated on paper,
but in practice they overlap constantly. A single project, like an industrial motor dashboard, can involve a
web frontend, an API backend, IoT hardware, and basic security practices all at once. Learning broadly
across these areas is what lets me build complete systems instead of just isolated pieces.
lesson: Broad, connected skills let you build end-to-end systems, not just individual components.
benefit: This is exactly what makes solo, full-system projects like the ones shared this month possible.

title: What's Next in My Developer Journey
hook: Thirty days of sharing my work taught me almost as much as building the projects did.
body:
Writing about these projects forced me to explain decisions I had previously only made instinctively. Going
forward, I want to go deeper into agentic AI, combine it more with computer vision and IoT projects, and
keep building practical systems rather than isolated demos. If any of these topics, from Flutter to FastAPI to
ESP32, are things you are also working on, I would genuinely like to hear about it.
lesson: Sharing your work publicly, even imperfectly, speeds up your own learning.
benefit: It also opens the door to feedback and collaboration I would not get by building quietly alone.
